::: {.callout-tip}
## Why This Matters
IISc's Centre for Nano Science and Engineering (CeNSE) houses India's main academic nanofabrication facility and, since 2022, the MeitY-funded Gallium Nitride Ecosystem Enabling Centre and Incubator (GEECI), run by IISc's incubation arm FSID. GEECI is a low-volume GaN development-line foundry for RF and power devices, and the site where AGNIT Semiconductors, an IISc spin-off, makes its chips.
:::

## What does this facility make?

Research-grade micro and nano devices (MEMS, photonics, novel semiconductor structures) for academic work, plus GaN epitaxial wafers and GaN RF and power transistors on the GEECI pilot line. AGNIT is scaling this line to 4-inch wafers and has begun pilot wafer exports.

## Why does it matter?

Besides training fabrication engineers, CeNSE is one of the few sites in India where GaN devices are made today; the other main one is the defence-run GAETEC in Hyderabad. Whether AGNIT can grow from this shared academic line into its own factory, as it says it wants to under Semicon 2.0, is a test of how lab-to-fab transitions work in India.

## Project Timeline

- **13 Mar 2022** — MoS Rajeev Chandrasekhar visits the MeitY-funded GaN technology centre (GEECI) at IISc
- **30 Jun 2023** — Oxford Instruments supplies GaN plasma-processing tools for the GEECI power and RF pilot line
- **17 Oct 2024** — AGNIT Semiconductors, which makes its chips at GEECI, raises a $3.5 million seed round
- **17 Mar 2026** — AGNIT raises a $2.6 million seed extension; targets 1 lakh GaN chips and says it wants its own GaN factory under Semicon 2.0
